label: text
text:
AFTERTHOUGHTS ON LOCAL CONCERT.
HONGKONG,

label: text
text: TIPS * FOR FUTURE.

label: text
text: Expert's Views On Possibilities of Music.

label: text
text: o [By Leung Kam-Cong]

label: text
text: Having been asked by the China Mail to give my views on the possibilities of broadcasting Chinese music I must begin by emphasising that I know practically nothing about radio beyond what I say and heard at Wednesday's test concert in which I was privileged to take a small part.

label: text
text: First of all I say emphatically that I think it of very little use to install apparatus in a theatre. The sounds, or music, or whatever one pleases to call it, emanating from a Chinese stage, are not in the least amenable to broad-lasting for entertainment, simply because of drama (or opera), is fundamentally different from that of the Occident.

label: text
text: "Here I should add that I am confining myself to the Cantonese theatre and music."

label: text
text:
Four Instruments Enough.
For broadcasting, whether as accompaniment to songs, or as selections, four instruments are ample. They should not be played at high pressure as is necessary on the stage because our theatrical acoustics are so poor and the audience so noisy.

label: text
text: For the singer's main guidance and support I would use the Woo Kum (a two-stringed fiddle of a mellow tone) instead of the Yee Yin (also a two-string-fiddle, but with thicker strings and therefore more penetrating), which occupies the place of "leader" both in a theatrical band and in an orchestra.

label: text
text: But nearer to the microphone, I suggest putting a dulcimer. A dulcimer is on the basis of a harp laid flat:—brass strings fastened on brass regulators which stand on a wooden sound-box, played by striking the strings with two thin strips of bamboo peel. Under ordinary auditory circumstances, the dulcimer is the sole accompaniment and it is played by the singer (soloist). Having brass strings which are very "soft" the dulcimer ought to be entirely free from blurs in reception, as the vibrations are so mild.

label: paragraph_title
text: A “Second Violin.”

label: text
text: Also closer to the microphone (i.e., between the dulcimer and the Woo Kum) I think there should be a Yee Woo, this also being a two string instrument, but even softer than the Woo Kum by virtue of its smaller drum at the base. The Yee Woo would be to the Woo Kum as the second violin to a first violin. The sounds of both fiddles are not unlike those of the violin.

label: text
text: At some distance from the microphone—because it is the loudest instrument—I think there ought to be a Hau Kwoon, this being a miniature clarionet minus the keys. It is best understood as a bamboo flute with reed mouthpiece, but only a few inches long. The general softness and smoothness of its tones would help and it is always pleasant to the Chinese ear.

label: text
text:
"Talking" Voice the Best.
The singer should be only a few inches from the microphone, singing almost directly into it, but with this one qualification. When we sing on the stage, or at concerts, we usually try to do our "loudest," for reasons given above. All singing for radio should be "generously modulated" in fact I would lay down that the normal "speaking" voice be used as I think it will be best heard on a receiving set, with or without loud speaker. The greatest difficulty in Cantonese singing is enunciation, or clarity of "words" as distinct from

label: paragraph_title
text: DESERTER.

label: text
text: AMERICAN SOLDIER FROM PHILIPPINES.

label: text
text: LANDED DESTITUTE.

label: text
text: Rufus Horak, aged 24, an American who on his own admission had deserted from the Philippines army, was charged before Major Willson this morning on two counts.

label: text
text:
The first count concerned the non-possession of a passport and the second his being without visible means of subsistence.
Sub-Inspector Fallon applied for the withdrawal of the first charge as he had instructions from the D.C.I., Mr. King, to ask for an order for the defendant's expulsion from the Colony. The defendant had given himself up to the Police after being in the Colony for some six days.

label: text
text:
In" reply to Major Willson, In-
spector Fallon said that it was
usual under the circumstances to
apply only for an order for deten-
tion.

label: text
text: In reply to another question, In-spector Fallon said that if such an order were made, the defendant would have liberty of action at certain hours. The principal object of the Police in regard to the accused was that they might have him continually under observation with a view to getting him deported when the opportunity arose. The Police were awaiting certain confirmation from Manila in the matter of photographs and papers of identification.

label: text
text: It was therefore decided to proceed on the charge of non-possession of passport on which defendant was convicted and sentenced to two months' hard labour.

label: paragraph_title
text: CANTON'S WAR.

label: paragraph_title
text: MILITARY REPORT FROM NORTH

label: text
text: A military report from the lunar front to Canton reads:—

label: text
text: At Yochow, 30,000 of the enemy (Wu Pei-fu's troops) are assembled but there is no central command.

label: text
text:
Sung Hok-kang has returned to Hunan and is reorganising the defeated forces of Ho Yao-chao (this leader being hostile to Canton, and having been previously defeated).
Various other military movements are reported such as the arrival of big numbers at Changsha (some days before the reported evacuation) with the requisite headquarters of brigades, divisions, etc.

label: text
text: Mention is also made of orders to the 4th and 6th divisions to take the field, and of a big conference at Cha Ling between the military and the civil population.

label: text
text: Russian Arms for Canton?

label: text
text: Further news of the extensive war movements in southern China, extending up to the Yangstze valley, is that Russia is sending more help to, Canton, and that other warlords are preparing to move.

label: text
text: General Chang Kai-Shek is reported to have ordered his 2nd and 3rd armies to advance; his objective being stated to be the entry of Fukien province by two routes.

label: text
text: The Fukien defence commissioner on the Kwangtung frontier is reported to have sent his artillery to Pingho.

label: text
text:
A cable to the "Wan Tsz Yat Po" says that another shipment of Russian arms and ammunitions is expected shortly at Canton.
A pro-Wu general is believed to have arrived at Amoy to cooperate with the Fukien tuchun and the Chinese naval vessels there in an offensive (against Kwangtung?).

label: text
text: Sun Chuan-fang has ordered the following movements of munitions: — light artillery, mountain artillery, rifles and ammunition from the Shanghai arsenal which is to work at night. Three car-loads (400,000 rounds) of ammunition from Lunghwa arsenal.—Kung Sheung Yat Po.

label: text
text: Peking is rumoured to have ordered an inquiry into the movements of M. Borodin, in Hunan province, where he accompanied general Chang Kai-shek.

label: text
text: SEIZURE ON BOARD THE FATSHAN.

label: text
text: SHIP'S PAINTER CHARGED.

label: text
text: Charged with unlawful possession of arms, the ammunition on board the "Fatshan" the ship's painter was brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy and formally remand-ed until Tuesday on the application of Detective Sub-Inspector Moss

label: text
text:
It had apparently been arranged that in the vicinity of Taishek Barrier a sampan was to await the arrival of the boat when the ingenious contrivances in which the arms were placed for floating purposes were to be lowered overboard and later picked up by the sampan which was to have a man's hat hoisted on a bamboo pole for purposes of identification. This sampan was in fact, passed by the "Fatshan" after the discovery had been made, also on the downward voyage, apparently still hopeful of the arms being lowered.
The first discovery of arms in the lamptrimmer's room led to a thorough search of the vessel and another consignment was discovered in a fish tub. As a result of information elicited in the course of enquiries the ship's painter was placed under arrest.
The seizure "consisted" of 20 Mauser Pistols, 12 Smith and Wesson revolvers and 3,200 rounds of ammunition.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRICE, $3.00 Per Month.

label: text
text: The seizure was made on the outward Voyage of the "Fatshan" from Hongkong on Thursday, discovery of a portion, of the arms being made when the boat was between Capsuimum and Castle Peak.

label: paragraph_title
text: ILLEGAL TRAFFIC.

label: text
text:
ARE TRAMP CARS A REAL
NECESSITY?

label: text
text: CORRESPONDENT'S VIEW.

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mail"]

label: text
text: Sir, — Your correspondent "Safety" evidently has a grudge against the tramp cars. flying for hire in Hongkong. I will ask him, the following questions, by your kind permission.

label: text
text: How does he know the C.S.P. has not taken steps to check the 'practice'?

label: text
text: Re drivers absconding: Do not drivers of cars other than tramps 'decamp' as well after a serious accident?

label: text
text: Re allegation of unlicensed drivers: This is a matter for the Police, no matter if the car is private, livery or tramp.

label: text
text: Do only 'ignorant' people patronise the tramp cars?

label: text
text: From the tone in which "Safety" writes I can only presume that he is a snob with his fleet of private cars. I have seen even real talpans ride in tramps, when necessity arose, so what has your correspondent to say now?

label: text
text: I find the tramps of much use on every occasion. From what I have seen, some of them seem to have taken out "public vehicle" licences. Accordingly, I presume that they pay the usual livery rates. Is any harm done then? The greater the competition, the lower the prices for the public. Since the tramps have "stands," regular or irregular, I suppose that they are permitted, or at least "known."

label: text
text:
"I live and let live is my motto.
Thanking you for inserting this
reply on behalf of 'ignorant'
drivers who are unable to answer
for themselves,"

label: text
text: Yours, etc.

label: paragraph_title
text: CASTLE PEAK.

label: paragraph_title
text:
TEMPORARILY OPEN BY
TUESDAY?

label: text
text: DIFFICULTIES ENCOUNTERED.

label: text
text: The work of clearing the one road yet remaining closed to the public since the recent heavy rain —that to Castle Peak—has been proceeding throughout the week and favourable progress has been made.

label: text
text: The work involved is" so considerable, however, that it has not been found possible to open the rond even temporarily for weekend travellers although the route via Taipo and Fanling is still available.

label: text
text:
A gap of some fifty to sixty feet in the embankment, leading to one of the bridges is having to be made good and this is the work which has led to the greatest difficulty experienced. It is anticipated that this work will be completed within four days' time.
There remains only about two days' work on other temporary clearances so it may be predicted with some certainty that given favourable conditions in the meantime, Castle Peak Road will be open to traffic by Tuesday.

label: paragraph_title
text: PICKETS SNUBBED:

label: text
text:
ALLEGED INTERVENTION OF
SOLDIERS.

label: text
text: HONGKONG PASSENGERS.

label: text
text: An “incident” in which a detachment alleged to be soldiers took high-handed action and supposedly snubbed the Strike Pickets' clearing office in Honans reported from Canton.

label: text
text: It may not be generally known that the strikers have the use of a high building on Honam island, on the opposite side of the river to Carlton city, where they issue permits for certain cargo and passports for passengers to and from Hongkong. A lookout is kept on the Hongkong steamboat from the top of the building.

label: text
text: This week it was alleged that a motor-boat took off from the steamboat one male passenger, eight ladies and a quantity of luggage. The motor-boat had permission to call on the steamboat but not to take off the passengers and their effects.

label: text
text: Action was taken and the motor-boat, passengers and luggage were detained. Three men, dressed like military officers, accompanied by ten or fifteen men armed with Mausers, are alleged to have gone to the clearing office, conducted themselves high-handedly, and finally to have made off with the motor-boat, passengers and luggage.

label: text
text: The report states that the “incident” has been brought to the notice of the Strike Executive and picket headquarters.

label: paragraph_title
text: ARBITRARY STEPS

label: paragraph_title
text: FOREIGN OWNED SCHOOLS IN CANTON.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHINESE AGITATION

label: text
text: Arbitrary steps are suggested in a resolution which was to have come before yesterday's meeting in Canton of the Executive Society on Education—steps which aim at the very root of "foreign" schools in Canton and territory.

label: text
text: The proposer is of the opinion that since the Nationalist Government is busy with the present war, decisive measures ought to be adopted by the Society. The proposals include:—

label: text
text: Administrative committees and positions of principals to be confined to Chinese (i.e., in schools now owned or controlled by foreigners).

label: text
text: Land and property vested in such institutions to be turned over to Chinese.

label: text
text: All schools managed by foreigners to be registered with the Government which will appoint one supervisor, from the educational departments, to be continually at the schools and to direct all matters and matters pertaining to administration.

label: text
text: (Syllabus, etc., to conform with Government regulations. Opposition to be overcome by forcible measures if necessary.)

label: paragraph_title
text: HAVE NO FEAR!

label: text
text: "WILD BEASTS" PASS THROUGH HONGKONG.

label: text
text: BUT DIDN'T STAY.

label: paragraph_title
text: ina, Tapir". Otter and Snakes.

label: text
text:
Residents who read this week's report of the Hongkong Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals may have noticed that under the heading of imports for July were 2 otters, 4 iguanas and 6 baskets of snakes.
In the course of their rounds, the inspectors of the Society 'care' even for the ferocious animals of the jungle, teaching

label: text
text: There was also in the monthly report a list under exports. But these strunge creatures were not mentioned in this section and the presumption was that they were kept here.

label: text
text: Such is not the case. One need have no fear that returning home late may mean an unwelcome welcome by stray iguana.

label: paragraph_title
text: Ate Iguana's Tall!

label: text
text: A gentleman who has roamed the seven seas spoke of having seen many members of this branch of the reptile family in the Philippine Islands. He also confessed to sharing in a meal off the tail the body being inedible. A guess that he hazard was that these iguanas were brought here to make a special brew of medicinal samshu, as an ingredient in Chinese wine like snakes, monkeys, etc.

label: text
text: Not knowing what an iguana was for, a "China Mail" reporter set out to make inquiries.

label: text
text: The four that came here were each six feet long, fully grown creatures. They awaited transhipment, and were not sent off till this month, hence the absence from the “exports.” The consignees are the Zoological Society of Japan, where the assembly is being gradually added to so that their “zoo” is now becoming well known.

label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong "Zoo."

label: text
text: The speaker on the subject of an iguana's tail, also told the "China Mail" man about a wild animal entrepot in Gilman Street, where a distributing agent received weird monsters from all parts of the world and delivered them to owners of travelling shows in all parts of China.

label: text
text: Seriously, however, an iguana, not unlike a chameleon, is the most aquatic of the lizard family. They live on marine vegetation, diving under water to do so; and they can stay under for some considerable time without coming to the surface to breathe.

label: text
text: Then somebody suggested that the otters may have been brought here by the Fanling Hunt. Such is not the case, the zoological gardens in Japan also being the destination in this case.

label: text
text: Snakes For Food.

label: text
text:
The “Mail” reporter also heard that a tapir arrived a few days ago, to be sent on to San Francisco.
Articles in previous issues of this paper have explained the uses to "which snakes are put by Chinese in this Colony and, of course, elsewhere. Snakes form an expensive item in diet—in fact more costly than a luxury. Even the poisonous variety have their value. The spleen is supposed to have great restorative attributes and the "meat" is considered a delicacy.

label: text
text: The import of snakes into Hongkong (from Canton "more far") has been restricted by the strike. But there is also a re-export business, Hongkong dealers sending on shipments to places where the Cantonese emigrate in any number.

label: text
text: As the winter is the snake feast season, it is thought that the batch of six baskets mentioned in the H.K.S.P.C.A. report were either for transhipment, or for making special snake gamshu.
